title: Scholars in Conversation
bigQuestion: When careful researchers read the same ancient documents and reach different conclusions, how can a student weigh their arguments fairly?

story.title: Two Stacks of Books
story.kicker: Two students read the same psalm, pile up commentaries by different scholars, and have to write one paper together.
paragraphs: It is late on a weekday evening in a university library. Two students, Dana and Marcus, share a long table near the reference shelves. Between them lies an open Bible, turned to Psalm 82. They are writing a joint paper for a class on the Psalms. They cannot agree on the first sentence.

Dana has stacked up books on the ancient Near East: E. Theodore Mullen's study of the divine council, Mark S. Smith's The Origins of Biblical Monotheism, and Michael Heiser's The Unseen Realm. She taps verse 1. God stands in the council of El, she says, and judges among the gods. That phrase has a known meaning at Ugarit. And verse 7 says they will die like humans. You say that only to someone who is not human.

Marcus has a different stack: older commentaries, a volume of Rashi in English, and a book of rabbinic readings. One reads the gods as judges in Israel, called gods because they judged in God's name. He points to John 10:34, where Jesus quotes the psalm. Some interpreters read Jesus as speaking about human leaders there. Then he slides over a third book that reads the psalm as spoken to Israel at Mount Sinai.

Dana writes three words across the top of a notepad: claim, evidence, counter-evidence. Under claim she writes her reading and his. Under evidence each of them lists verses, manuscripts and parallels. Under counter-evidence each has to write the strongest point against their own view. Marcus groans, then laughs, and starts writing.

By closing time the paper still has two readings, but each one is stated fairly. They have also noticed that their authors agree on some things, such as what the Hebrew words say, and argue about others. This chapter follows the researchers who study these texts, and maps where they agree and where they part ways.
story.think: Why might writing the strongest point against your own view make your paper better?

lessons.title: From Ugarit to the Psalms
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars such as Frank Moore Cross and E. Theodore Mullen studied the divine council decades before popular books made it widely known.
reading: The Hebrew Bible has several scenes set in a heavenly court. In 1 Kings 22:19–22 the prophet Micaiah sees the LORD on his throne with the host of heaven around him, discussing a plan. Job 1–2 opens with the sons of God presenting themselves before the LORD. In Isaiah 6 the prophet hears the question, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Psalm 82 names the council outright.

After the Ugaritic tablets were read in the 1930s, scholars could compare these scenes with the assembly of El. Frank Moore Cross discussed the council in Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic (1973). E. Theodore Mullen gave it a full study in The Assembly of the Gods: The Divine Council in Canaanite and Early Hebrew Literature (1980). He set the Ugaritic assembly beside the council scenes of the Hebrew Bible and traced what was shared and what was changed.

So the idea of a *divine council* is not the view of one writer. It is a standard topic in the study of the Hebrew Bible. Most scholars agree the texts use council imagery. What they debate is what that imagery meant to Israel's writers, and whether it changed over time. The next lessons follow that debate.

words.d: an assembly of heavenly beings around a chief god, found in Ugaritic texts and, many scholars argue, in the Hebrew Bible
a biblical phrase for the heavenly beings around God's throne, as in 1 Kings 22:19
a later writing that explains or studies a primary source, such as a commentary or a scholarly book
the ancient document itself, such as a scroll, a tablet or a book of the Bible

look.title: Micaiah's Vision
look.text: I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left.
look.prompt: What details in this verse make it look like a royal court? Why would scholars call it a council scene?

check.q: Which scholar wrote The Assembly of the Gods (1980) on the divine council?
check.why: Mullen's 1980 study compared the Ugaritic assembly with council scenes in the Hebrew Bible.

check.q: In 1 Kings 22:19, what does the prophet Micaiah see?
choices: The LORD on his throne with the host of heaven around him
A storm breaking the cedars of Lebanon
Enoch taken up in a chariot
check.why: Micaiah describes the LORD enthroned with the host of heaven on his right and left.

check.q: On which point do most scholars agree?
choices: The council idea was invented in 2015
Psalm 82 is about Israel at Sinai
The Hebrew Bible uses divine council imagery
Israel's writers copied Ugarit word for word
check.why: Most scholars accept the council imagery; they debate how to explain it.

lessons.title: One God and the Council
lessons.mainIdea: Mark S. Smith reads Israel's monotheism as developing over time, while Michael Heiser read the canon as one God above a council of lesser beings.
reading: Isaiah 45:5 has God say: I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me (KJV). Yet Psalm 82 and Deuteronomy 32 speak of gods or sons of God. How do these fit together? Scholars who study the history of Israel's religion give different answers. The question involves dating texts, reading Ugarit, and deciding what an ancient writer meant by a god.

Mark S. Smith is a leading scholar of Ugarit and the Hebrew Bible. In The Early History of God (1990) and The Origins of Biblical Monotheism (2001), he argues that Israel's religion grew over centuries from a Canaanite setting. In his view, clear statements of *monotheism*, the belief that only one god exists, come in texts from around the Babylonian exile, such as Isaiah 40–55.

Michael Heiser, in his 2004 dissertation and later The Unseen Realm (2015), read the texts as they stand in the canon. He argued they show one God who is unlike all others, with a council of lesser *elohim* he created. He read Isaiah 45:5 as a claim that none compares with the LORD, not a denial that other heavenly beings exist. Smith and many others read such verses as denying that other gods exist. Each reading takes the Hebrew seriously; they differ on method.

words.d: the belief that only one god exists
a Hebrew word used for the God of Israel and also for other beings of the unseen world
the list of books a community accepts as Scripture
the study of how beliefs and practices changed over time

look.title: One Verse, Two Readings
look.text: Isaiah 45:5, King James Version (1611): I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me. Reading 1 (Smith and many others): the verse denies that any other gods exist. Reading 2 (Heiser): the verse says no other being compares to the LORD, while other heavenly beings still exist.
look.prompt: What evidence from elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible would you need to decide between these readings?

check.q: What does Mark S. Smith argue about Israel's monotheism?
choices: It was invented by the rabbis after 70 CE
It came directly from Mesopotamia's apkallu
It developed over centuries from a Canaanite setting
It is found fully formed at Ugarit
check.why: Smith's books trace a development, with clear monotheistic statements around the exile.

check.q: How did Heiser read Isaiah 45:5?
choices: As a later addition to Isaiah
As proof that Psalm 82 is about human judges
As a verse about the Watchers
As saying no other being compares with the LORD
check.why: Heiser read such verses as claims of incomparability, not denials that other heavenly beings exist.

check.q: What is monotheism?
choices: A reading that treats a story as allegory
The belief in a council of equal gods
The belief that only one god exists
check.why: Monotheism means belief in only one god; scholars debate when and how Israel's texts express it.

lessons.title: Deuteronomy 32:8 and the Text Critics
lessons.mainIdea: A Dead Sea Scroll and the Septuagint point to sons of God in Deuteronomy 32:8, a reading most text critics now accept over the Masoretic sons of Israel.
reading: Deuteronomy 32:8 in the King James Version reads: When the most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel. That last phrase follows the *Masoretic Text*, the standard Hebrew text behind most Bibles.

A copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran, called 4QDeut j, is centuries older than the oldest complete Masoretic manuscripts. At this verse it reads sons of God. The *Septuagint* points the same way; most of its copies read angels of God. To choose between readings, text critics ask which one best explains how the others arose. A scribe is more likely to smooth a puzzling phrase than to create one. Many judge that sons of God was changed to sons of Israel, not the reverse.

This method is called *textual criticism*. Emanuel Tov's handbook, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible (first English edition 1992), sets out its tools. Several modern translations now follow the scroll here. Scholars with very different views accept this reading, among them Smith and Heiser, who argued for it in a 2001 journal article. Some still defend sons of Israel, linking it to the seventy of Jacob's family in Genesis 46:27.

words.d: the standard Hebrew text of the Hebrew Bible, copied and marked by scribes called Masoretes, about 600–1000 CE
the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun in the third century BCE
the careful comparison of manuscripts to find the most likely earliest wording; criticism here means judging, not finding fault
a Dead Sea Scroll copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4 that reads sons of God in 32:8

look.title: Three Witnesses, One Verse
look.text: King James Version (1611), from the Masoretic Text: according to the number of the children of Israel. Dead Sea Scroll 4QDeut j: according to the number of the sons of God. Most Septuagint copies: according to the number of the angels of God.
look.prompt: Two of the three witnesses agree in meaning. What else would a text critic want to know before choosing a reading?

check.q: What does the Qumran scroll 4QDeut j read in Deuteronomy 32:8?
check.why: 4QDeut j reads sons of God, where the Masoretic Text has sons of Israel.

check.q: Which rule of thumb helps text critics choose between readings?
choices: Prefer the reading that best explains how the others arose
Always follow the most popular translation
Choose the reading that sounds best in English
check.why: Text critics ask which reading best explains the others; scribes tended to smooth hard phrases.

check.q: Which text lies behind the King James reading children of Israel in Deuteronomy 32:8?
check.why: The KJV follows the Masoretic Text here.

lessons.title: Milik and the Cave 4 Fragments
lessons.mainIdea: J. T. Milik's 1976 edition of the Aramaic Enoch fragments showed that most of 1 Enoch was being copied by about 200 BCE, though not the Parables.
reading: Before 1947, scholars knew 1 Enoch mainly from Ge'ez manuscripts and some Greek pieces. Many dated its parts to the second or first century BCE. Then the Qumran caves gave up Aramaic fragments. J. T. Milik, a Polish scholar on the team that worked on the Cave 4 scrolls, published them in The Books of Enoch: Aramaic Fragments of Qumrân Cave 4 (1976).

Milik's edition showed copies of the Book of the Watchers, the Astronomical Book, the Dream Visions and the Epistle. He dated some of the oldest copies, including one of the Astronomical Book and one of the Book of the Watchers, to around 200 BCE or a little after. If a book was already being copied then, it must have been written earlier. This pushed the oldest parts of 1 Enoch back into the third century BCE.

One part was missing: the Parables (chapters 37–71). Milik argued that the Parables were a much later Christian work, from around 270 CE. Most scholars have not followed that date. Many now place the Parables around the turn of the era, in the first century BCE or first century CE. The debate shows how a new *manuscript* find can settle one question and open another.

words.d: a hand-written copy of a text
a language related to Hebrew, widely spoken in the ancient Near East; parts of Daniel and many Qumran texts are in it
dating a manuscript by the style of its handwriting

Copies of the Astronomical Book (4QEnastr a–d)
look.cite: J. T. Milik, The Books of Enoch (1976), described in our own words
look.prompt: What does the zero in the last row suggest? Why are scholars still careful about drawing a firm conclusion from a missing text?

check.q: What did Milik publish in 1976?
choices: The first English translation of Josephus
The Aramaic Enoch fragments from Qumran Cave 4
check.why: Milik's The Books of Enoch published the Aramaic fragments from Cave 4.

check.why: No fragments of the Parables have been found among the scrolls.

check.q: What date did Milik propose for the Parables, a date most scholars have not followed?
choices: Around 270 CE, as a Christian work
check.why: Milik argued for a late Christian date; many scholars now place the Parables around the turn of the era.

lessons.title: VanderKam and the Seventh from Adam
lessons.mainIdea: James VanderKam (1984) traced how the Enoch tradition grew, and compared Enoch, seventh from Adam, with Enmeduranki, the seventh king before the flood in Mesopotamian lists.
reading: Genesis 5 places Enoch seventh in the line from Adam and gives him 365 years, the number of days in a solar year. It says he walked with God. James VanderKam, in Enoch and the Growth of an Apocalyptic Tradition (1984), asked why Jewish writers built so much on so few lines.

VanderKam pointed to Mesopotamian lists of kings who ruled before the flood. The seventh, Enmeduranki, was linked to the sun god and to secret knowledge about reading the future. VanderKam argued that Jewish writers knew such traditions. They shaped Enoch as a Jewish answer: the seventh man, linked to the sun's year, who received true knowledge from God's angels rather than from divination.

VanderKam also traced the order of the Enoch books. He treated the Astronomical Book and the Book of the Watchers as the oldest, from the third century BCE, with later parts added over time. That is why scholars speak of the growth of the Enoch tradition. Later, VanderKam and George Nickelsburg together published 1 Enoch: A New Translation (2004), now widely used by students.

words.d: in Mesopotamian king lists, the seventh king before the flood, linked to the sun god and to secret knowledge
writing that reveals hidden things, such as heaven, the end of the age or the meaning of history, often through visions
a body of stories and teachings handed down and added to over time

look.title: Two Sevenths

look.prompt: What likenesses do you see? Using Sandmel's warning about parallels, what would you need to show before saying one tradition shaped the other?

check.q: Which Mesopotamian figure did VanderKam compare with Enoch?
choices: Enmeduranki, the seventh king before the flood
Oannes, the sage from the sea
check.why: VanderKam compared Enoch, seventh from Adam, with Enmeduranki, seventh king before the flood.

check.q: Why is the number 365 in Genesis 5:23 important to this comparison?
choices: It matches the days of a solar year, linking Enoch with the sun
It is the number of Watchers in 1 Enoch
It is the year Ugarit was destroyed
It is the number of nations in Genesis 10
check.why: Enoch lives 365 years, the number of days in a solar year.

check.q: Which two parts of 1 Enoch did VanderKam treat as the oldest?
choices: The Epistle and the Dream Visions
The Astronomical Book and the Book of the Watchers
The Dream Visions and the Parables
check.why: VanderKam placed the Astronomical Book and the Book of the Watchers in the third century BCE.

lessons.title: Nickelsburg's Commentary
lessons.mainIdea: George Nickelsburg's commentary (2001) reads 1 Enoch 6–11 as two woven strands and has suggested that the giants' violence reflects the wars of its own time.
reading: George W. E. Nickelsburg's 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary (Hermeneia, 2001) covers chapters 1–36 and 81–108 verse by verse. It is one of the most detailed studies of the Book of the Watchers. Like many scholars, Nickelsburg sees in chapters 6–11 two strands woven together. In one, Shemihazah leads the Watchers, who take wives and father giants. In the other, Asael (called Azazel in Charles's translation) teaches forbidden arts.

Nickelsburg has also asked why such a story would be told when it was. After Alexander the Great died in 323 BCE, his generals fought long wars over his empire, and the land of Israel lay between them. Nickelsburg has suggested that the giants, who claim descent from heavenly beings and fill the earth with violence, mirror those warring rulers. Some Greek kings in this period did claim divine descent.

Other scholars stress different settings, such as disputes among priests or the pull of Greek learning. A reader can hold these views side by side. Each asks what the story meant to its first hearers. None of them requires a reader to decide whether Watchers existed. That question belongs to faith communities, not to the historian's method.

words.d: a scholarly book that explains a text passage by passage
one of several older stories or sources woven together in a text
the period after Alexander the Great, about 323 to 30 BCE, when Greek culture spread across the Near East
the Aramaic spelling of the Watchers' leader; Charles's translation spells it Semjaza

look.title: A Commentator's Proposal
look.text: Nickelsburg suggests that the Book of the Watchers speaks to its own age. The giants, born of heavenly fathers and filling the earth with bloodshed, can be read as a picture of the rulers who fought over Alexander's empire, some of whom claimed descent from gods.
look.cite: George W. E. Nickelsburg, 1 Enoch 1: A Commentary (2001), described in our own words
look.prompt: What evidence from the text and from history would support this reading? What would a reader who stresses a different setting say?

check.q: What does Nickelsburg see woven together in 1 Enoch 6–11?
choices: A Ugaritic poem and a psalm
Two strands, one about Shemihazah and one about Asael
check.why: Nickelsburg, with many scholars, sees a Shemihazah strand and an Asael strand.

check.q: What historical setting has Nickelsburg suggested for the giants story?
choices: The time of Moses at Sinai
The fall of Ugarit around 1185 BCE
The wars among Alexander's successors after 323 BCE
check.why: He has suggested the giants mirror the warring rulers of the early Hellenistic age.

check.q: Which book did Nickelsburg and VanderKam publish together in 2004?
choices: The Book of Giants from Qumran
check.why: Nickelsburg and VanderKam published 1 Enoch: A New Translation in 2004.

lessons.title: Where Unclean Spirits Come From
lessons.mainIdea: Archie Wright, Loren Stuckenbruck and Michael Heiser have each traced how 1 Enoch 15's giant spirits shaped later ideas of unclean spirits, while other readers see demons as fallen angels.
reading: The Gospels speak of *unclean spirits*. In Mark 1:23–27, in the synagogue at Capernaum, a man cries out, and Jesus commands the unclean spirit to leave. The man is a member of that town and that synagogue, and the story ends with him free and the crowd amazed. The Gospels do not explain where such spirits came from. Researchers have asked what background their first readers had.

Archie T. Wright, in The Origin of Evil Spirits (2005), studied how early Jewish writers received Genesis 6:1–4. He argued that the Book of the Watchers, with its giant spirits in chapter 15, shaped later Jewish thinking about evil spirits. Loren Stuckenbruck's essays in The Myth of Rebellious Angels (2014) also trace how the Watchers and giants traditions were used in Second Temple texts and the New Testament.

Michael Heiser, in The Unseen Realm (2015) and Demons (2020), held that demons in the Gospels are the spirits of the dead giants, following 1 Enoch 15. Many Christian readers through history have instead understood demons as fallen angels themselves, cast out of heaven with Satan. Both readings appear among careful scholars. None of these researchers linked unclean spirits to illness, disability or how a person's mind works.

words.d: the Gospels' phrase for harmful spirits; many scholars trace part of its background to 1 Enoch 15
the era of the rebuilt Jerusalem temple, about 516 BCE to 70 CE
how later readers took up, used and changed an earlier text
the study of what a tradition teaches about demons

look.title: From Enoch to the Gospels
look.text: 1 Enoch 15:8–10 (described): the spirits of the giants, born of spirits and flesh, will remain on earth as evil spirits. Mark 1:23–27 (described): in the synagogue at Capernaum, Jesus commands an unclean spirit to leave a man, and the man goes on with his life among his neighbors.
look.prompt: Mark does not mention Enoch. What would a researcher need to show to argue that Mark's first readers knew the Enoch story? What else could explain the phrase unclean spirit?

check.q: What did Archie Wright study in The Origin of Evil Spirits (2005)?
choices: The rabbinic debate over two powers
How early Jewish writers received Genesis 6:1–4
check.why: Wright traced how the Genesis 6 story, through 1 Enoch, shaped ideas of evil spirits.

check.q: Where did Heiser, following 1 Enoch 15, say demons came from?
choices: The spirits of the dead giants
check.why: Heiser held that the Gospels' demons are the disembodied spirits of the giants.

check.q: What other reading of demons have many Christian readers held?
choices: That they are the Ugaritic gods
That they are fallen angels themselves
That they are the Watchers' teachers of writing
check.why: Many Christian readers have seen demons as angels who fell with Satan.

lessons.title: How the Watchers Story Traveled
lessons.mainIdea: Annette Yoshiko Reed (2005) traced how the Watchers story was embraced by early Christian writers, set aside by most rabbis, and later replaced in much of the church by the Sethite reading.
reading: Jude 14–15 quotes a prophecy of Enoch that closely matches 1 Enoch 1:9. Early Christian writers used the Watchers story too. Justin Martyr, writing in Rome around 150 CE, said in his Second Apology that angels broke God's order, loved women and fathered children who are called demons. Tertullian, around 200 CE, defended the book of Enoch as Scripture in On the Apparel of Women, though he knew some did not accept it.

Annette Yoshiko Reed traced this history in Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity (2005). She showed that the Watchers story was widely read in the Second Temple period. Then, in different ways, both rabbinic Judaism and much of the Christian church moved it to the edges. Rabbinic sources such as Genesis Rabbah read the sons of God as sons of judges or nobles. Only the Ethiopian church kept 1 Enoch in its Bible.

In the church, the *Sethite view* spread. It reads the sons of God as the godly line of Seth and the daughters of men as the line of Cain. Julius Africanus held it in the early 200s. Augustine discussed it in The City of God in the early 400s. Many Protestant commentators have held it since. Reed's work helps readers see that a story's place in a tradition can change over centuries.

words.d: the reading of Genesis 6 in which the sons of God are Seth's descendants, not heavenly beings
early Christian writers of roughly the first to eighth centuries
an early rabbinic commentary on Genesis, about the 400s CE
a series of English translations of early Christian writers, published 1885–87, now in the public domain

look.title: Justin Martyr on the Angels
look.text: God gave the care of humans and of things under heaven to angels. But the angels broke this order. They were captured by love of women and fathered children, who are those called demons.
look.cite: Justin Martyr, Second Apology 5, paraphrased after the Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1 (1885)
look.prompt: Which ancient document does Justin's account most resemble? What does that suggest about what he had read or heard?

check.q: What did Annette Yoshiko Reed trace in her 2005 book?
choices: How the Ugaritic alphabet was deciphered
How the Watchers story was received and later set aside in Judaism and Christianity
check.why: Reed's Fallen Angels traces the reception of Enochic literature in both traditions.

check.q: Which early Christian writer defended the book of Enoch as Scripture?
check.why: Tertullian defended Enoch in On the Apparel of Women, around 200 CE.

check.q: In the Sethite view, who are the sons of God in Genesis 6?
check.why: The Sethite view, held by Julius Africanus and discussed by Augustine, reads them as Seth's line.

lessons.title: Two Powers in Heaven
lessons.mainIdea: Alan Segal (1977) studied rabbinic warnings against belief in two powers in heaven, and Heiser argued that the pattern behind that belief goes back to the Hebrew Bible.
reading: Daniel 7:9–14 describes a throne scene. The Ancient of Days takes his seat, and one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and receives everlasting rule. In Exodus 3 the angel of the LORD appears in the bush, and then God speaks from it. In Exodus 23:20–21 God says his name is in the angel he sends. Ancient readers asked how these figures relate to God.

In 1977 Alan Segal published Two Powers in Heaven: Early Rabbinic Reports about Christianity and Gnosticism. He studied rabbinic passages that warn against people who say there are two powers in heaven. Segal argued that the idea was older than the warnings. It grew from how some Jews read passages like Daniel 7, and the rabbis came to treat it as a serious error.

Heiser built on Segal in his dissertation (2004) and The Unseen Realm (2015). He argued that the Hebrew Bible itself has a visible and an invisible LORD figure, and that early Christians read Jesus into that pattern. Rabbinic Judaism reads these passages differently. The *Shema*, Deuteronomy 6:4, declares that the LORD is one. The angel of the LORD is read as a created messenger speaking in God's name.

words.d: a belief the early rabbis rejected: that a second divine figure shared heaven's rule
the title of the enthroned figure in Daniel 7:9
Deuteronomy 6:4, the central Jewish declaration that the LORD is one
a figure in the Hebrew Bible who speaks for God and sometimes as God, as in Exodus 3

look.title: Daniel's Throne Scene
look.text: Daniel 7:9–14, described in our own words: thrones are set up and the Ancient of Days takes his seat, with white clothing and hair like wool. Then one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven. He is brought before the Ancient of Days and given rule that will never end.
look.prompt: How might a rabbinic reader, a Christian reader and a historian like Segal each explain the one like a son of man?

check.q: What did Alan Segal study in Two Powers in Heaven (1977)?
choices: Rabbinic warnings against belief in two powers in heaven
check.why: Segal studied rabbinic reports that condemn a belief in two powers in heaven.

check.q: In Daniel 7, who comes with the clouds of heaven?
choices: One like a son of man
check.why: Daniel 7:13 describes one like a son of man coming with the clouds.

check.q: How does rabbinic Judaism read the angel of the LORD?
choices: As a second god equal to the LORD
As a created messenger speaking in God's name
check.why: Rabbinic tradition holds to the oneness of God in the Shema and reads the angel as a messenger.

lessons.title: A Framework and Its Critics
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser joined Genesis 3, 6 and 11 into three rebellions and a Deuteronomy 32 worldview; readers find it clarifying or too tightly systematized.
reading: Genesis 3 tells of the serpent in Eden. Genesis 6:1–4 tells of the sons of God and the daughters of men. Genesis 11 tells of Babel and the scattering of the nations. In the Bible these are separate stories. Heiser, in The Unseen Realm (2015), read them as three rebellions: in Eden, before the flood, and at Babel.

He tied the third to Deuteronomy 32:8–9, read with the Qumran scroll. In his view, after Babel God placed the nations under members of his council and kept Israel as his own. Psalm 82 then shows those rulers judged for ruling unjustly. Heiser called this the *Deuteronomy 32 worldview*. He used it to read Daniel 10's princes of Persia and Greece and Paul's language of rulers and authorities.

Other readers raise questions. Genesis does not call Babel a rebellion in heaven, and Deuteronomy 32:8 does not say the sons of God rebelled. Psalm 82 does not say when their wrongdoing began. Some reviewers say the framework joins texts from different books and centuries into a tighter system than any one of them states. Supporters reply that it explains passages that otherwise seem scattered. Christian tradition has more often spoken of one fall of angels and one fall of humanity.

words.d: a large pattern an interpreter uses to connect and explain many passages
Heiser's name for the idea that God placed the nations under lesser heavenly beings and kept Israel for himself
Heiser's reading of Eden, Genesis 6 and Babel as three rebellions in the unseen realm
to arrange many ideas into one ordered system

look.title: Where the Three Stories Stand
rows: Eden and the serpent, Genesis chapter
The sons of God, Genesis chapter
Babel and the nations, Genesis chapter
look.cite: Genesis; Heiser, The Unseen Realm (2015), described in our own words
look.prompt: The three stories span nine chapters. What would a critic say about linking them as one pattern? What would a supporter answer?

check.q: Which three Genesis stories make up the three-rebellions framework?
choices: Eden, the sons of God, and Babel
check.why: The framework joins Genesis 3, 6:1–4 and 11.

check.q: Which passage gives the Deuteronomy 32 worldview its name and base?
choices: Deuteronomy 32:8–9, read with the Qumran scroll
check.why: The framework rests on the sons of God reading of Deuteronomy 32:8 and Israel as God's portion in 32:9.

check.q: What is one criticism of the three-rebellions framework?
choices: It rejects the Dead Sea Scrolls
It joins texts into a tighter system than any one of them states
It depends on the Ugaritic alphabet
It ignores the book of Genesis
check.why: Critics note that Genesis and Deuteronomy do not themselves call Babel a heavenly rebellion.

lessons.title: Jewish Readings Through Time
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish readers of Genesis 6 moved from angels in 1 Enoch, Jubilees and Philo to rulers and judges in the Targum, Genesis Rabbah and Rashi.
reading: There is no single Jewish view of Genesis 6. Books written by Jews in the Second Temple period, such as 1 Enoch and Jubilees, read the sons of God as angels. So did Philo and Josephus in the first century CE. Some Dead Sea Scrolls, such as the Damascus Document, speak of the Watchers who fell.

Later rabbinic tradition mostly took another path. The *Targum* Onkelos, an Aramaic translation of the Torah, renders sons of God in Genesis 6:2 as sons of the great ones, meaning nobles. The *midrash* Genesis Rabbah reads it as sons of judges. Rashi, the great commentator of the eleventh century, explains them as sons of princes and judges. In this line, the wrong in Genesis 6 is the abuse of power by the mighty.

Jewish tradition still has a heavenly court. Genesis Rabbah, on Genesis 1:26, pictures God consulting the ministering angels before creating humans. What rabbinic Judaism rejects is a second being sharing God's rule. Today Jewish communities read these passages in many ways. A fair study notes the variety and does not treat any one period as the whole of Jewish reading.

words.d: an Aramaic translation of a book of the Hebrew Bible, often with added explanation
rabbinic interpretation of Scripture, and the books that collect it
Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040–1105), a French Jewish commentator on the Bible and Talmud
the first five books of the Hebrew Bible

look.title: Genesis 6:2 Across Jewish History
look.text: 1 Enoch (oldest parts, 3rd century BCE): angels, called Watchers. Jubilees (2nd century BCE): angels. Philo and Josephus (1st century CE): angels. Targum Onkelos (early centuries CE): sons of the great ones. Genesis Rabbah (about 400s CE): sons of judges. Rashi (11th century CE): sons of princes and judges.
look.prompt: What change do you see over time? What might explain why readings shifted? Which researcher in this chapter studied that shift?

check.q: How does Targum Onkelos render sons of God in Genesis 6:2?
check.why: Targum Onkelos reads sons of the great ones, meaning nobles.

check.q: Which Jewish writers read the sons of God as angels?
choices: The authors of 1 Enoch and Jubilees, and Philo
check.why: Second Temple texts and Philo read angels; later rabbinic texts read rulers or judges.

check.q: What is a midrash?
choices: A copy of 1 Enoch in Ge'ez
Rabbinic interpretation of Scripture and the books that collect it
A Greek translation of the Torah
check.why: Genesis Rabbah is a midrash, a rabbinic commentary on Genesis.

lessons.title: Claim, Evidence, Counter-Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: A fair reader states each claim plainly, lists its evidence and its hardest counter-evidence, and sorts what is widely agreed from what is still debated.
reading: Every interpretation makes a *claim*. The claim should fit in one sentence so it can be tested: The gods in Psalm 82 are members of a heavenly council. Or: The gods in Psalm 82 are human judges. Next comes *evidence*: a verse, a word, a manuscript, a parallel. For the council reading, evidence includes adat el in verse 1, the Ugaritic parallels and die like men in verse 7.

Then comes *counter-evidence*, the facts hardest for the claim to explain. For the council reading, a reader might cite John 10:34–35, where Jesus speaks of those to whom the word of God came. For the human-judges reading, the council setting and die like men are the hardest facts. Stating the case against your own view is not weakness. It makes a conclusion trustworthy. Some teachers call this *steelmanning*.

Last comes sorting. Widely agreed: the Bible has council scenes; the Qumran scroll reads sons of God in Deuteronomy 32:8; Jude 14–15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9; most of 1 Enoch is older than 150 BCE. Still debated: how monotheism developed, where demons come from, the three rebellions, the date of the Parables. Keeping the lists apart prevents a common mistake: treating a debated claim as settled, or a settled one as mere opinion.

words.d: a statement an interpreter argues for, put plainly so it can be tested
specific facts that support a claim, such as a verse, a word or a manuscript
the facts that are hardest for a claim to explain
stating an opposing view in its strongest form before judging it

look.title: Sort the Claims
look.text: 1. The Hebrew Bible contains council scenes such as 1 Kings 22. 2. A Dead Sea Scroll reads sons of God in Deuteronomy 32:8. 3. Jude 14–15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9. 4. Genesis 3, 6 and 11 describe three rebellions in the unseen realm. 5. The demons of the Gospels are the spirits of the giants. 6. The Parables of Enoch were written around 270 CE.
look.prompt: Put each claim in one of two lists: widely agreed or still debated. Give a reason for two of your choices.

check.q: What is counter-evidence?
choices: The facts that are hardest for a claim to explain
A list of scholars who share a view
Evidence that agrees with every reading
check.why: Counter-evidence is what a claim struggles to explain; stating it makes a conclusion trustworthy.

check.q: Which of these is widely agreed among scholars?
choices: The demons are the spirits of the giants
The Parables were written around 270 CE
check.why: Scholars agree that Jude quotes 1 Enoch 1:9; the other claims are debated.

check.q: What does steelmanning ask a reader to do?
choices: Attack the weakest version of a view
State the opposing view in its strongest form first
Quote a modern book word for word
check.why: Steelmanning means building the strongest version of a view before judging it.

review.q: Which two scholars studied the divine council in Canaanite and Hebrew texts before 1981?
choices: William Whiston and C. D. Yonge
Archie Wright and Annette Yoshiko Reed
Frank Moore Cross and E. Theodore Mullen
review.why: Cross (1973) and Mullen (1980) wrote on the council long before recent popular books.

review.q: Why do most text critics prefer sons of God in Deuteronomy 32:8?
choices: A Qumran scroll and the Septuagint support it, and it best explains the change
It appears in the King James Version
review.why: 4QDeut j and the Septuagint point to sons of God, and scribes tended to smooth hard readings.

review.q: What did Milik's 1976 edition show about 1 Enoch?
choices: The Parables were the oldest part
Most of its parts were being copied in Aramaic by about 200 BCE
It was first written in Ge'ez in 1773
It was unknown before the Middle Ages
review.why: Milik's fragments pushed the oldest parts of 1 Enoch back into the third century BCE.

review.q: Whose book traced how the Watchers story was embraced and then set aside by Jews and Christians?
review.why: Reed's Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity (2005) traces that history.

review.q: Which reading of demons follows 1 Enoch 15?
choices: They are the spirits of the dead giants
They are the sons of Seth
They are the seventy sons of Athirat
review.why: 1 Enoch 15 says the giants' spirits became evil spirits; Wright, Stuckenbruck and Heiser trace that idea.

review.q: How do Smith and Heiser differ on Isaiah 45:5?
choices: Smith reads it as about Ugarit; Heiser as about Babylon
Both read it as about the Watchers
Smith reads a denial of other gods; Heiser read a claim that none compares with the LORD
Neither thinks it is in Isaiah
review.why: The two scholars read no God beside me in different ways.

review.q: Which Jewish reading of Genesis 6:2 appears in Genesis Rabbah?
review.why: Genesis Rabbah reads the sons of God as sons of judges.

review.q: Which statement is still debated among scholars?
choices: That 1 Kings 22 has a council scene
That 4QDeut j reads sons of God in 32:8
review.why: The development of monotheism is debated; the other statements are widely accepted.
